exam.step: Look for tongue lateral bite marks
exam.positive: Lateral tongue biting is specific for a generalised seizure
A prolonged recovery supports seizure over syncope
Focal deficit suggests a structural cause

After referral, to classify and find a cause

conditions.name: Seizure / epilepsy
conditions.summary: Abnormal electrical discharge in the brain. Often with tongue biting, incontinence and a confused drowsy period afterwards that separates it from a simple faint.

exam.positive: Blurred disc margins with loss of venous pulsation

exam.step: Test visual fields and blind spot

labs.test: Do not perform lumbar puncture before imaging

triage.label: Emergency
triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

conditions.summary: A mass or swelling inside the skull. The headache is worst on waking, worse on coughing or bending, and comes with vomiting and progressive neurological change.

conditions.name: Intracerebral haemorrhage

triage.label: Emergency
triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

conditions.summary: Bleeding into brain tissue. Looks like a stroke but with more headache, vomiting and rapid deterioration, and is far more likely on anticoagulants.

exam.positive: Inability to place chin on chest

labs.confirms: Baseline and excludes hypoglycaemia before transfer

labs.test: Non-contrast CT head within one hour
Lumbar puncture at 12 hours if CT negative
Clotting screen and group and save

conditions.summary: Bleeding around the brain from a ruptured aneurysm. Announced by a headache that reaches full force in under a minute, like being struck on the head.

Lumbar puncture at 12 hours if CT negative

exam.positive: Inability to place chin on chest
Guides whether CT precedes lumbar puncture

labs.test: Blood cultures then immediate IV antibiotics

Cell count, protein, glucose, culture and PCR

labs.test: CT head first only if focal signs, seizures or reduced GCS

conditions.name: Bacterial meningitis

triage.label: Emergency
triage.action: Call emergency services or go to an emergency department now

conditions.summary: Infection of the membranes around the brain. Fever, severe headache and a neck too stiff to bend, sometimes with a rash that does not fade under pressure.
workup: Blood cultures then immediate IV antibiotics

exam.positive: Brief (<5 min), generalised, with full recovery within an hour is typical of a simple febrile seizure

exam.step: Look for a source of the fever
exam.positive: Ear, throat, chest, urine -- guides treatment of the underlying infection
Neck stiffness, photophobia, non-blanching rash or focal neurology point away from a simple febrile seizure and need urgent assessment for meningitis/encephalitis instead

labs.test: Clinical assessment directed at the fever's source
labs.confirms: Usually sufficient for a simple febrile seizure
Only if red flags present (prolonged/focal seizure, incomplete recovery, meningism)

conditions.name: Febrile seizure
conditions.summary: A seizure in a child aged roughly 6 months to 5 years, triggered by a rapidly rising fever, typically brief and generalised with rapid, full recovery afterwards -- one of the most common and most anxiety-provoking paediatric presentations, and usually benign. A seizure lasting over 5 minutes, focal features, or incomplete recovery within an hour need emergency assessment, and any FIRST seizure should still be seen urgently to exclude meningitis or another cause.
workup: Find and treat the fever's source (examination, urine/throat/other cultures as indicated)
Lumbar puncture/neuroimaging only if red flags are present, not routinely for a simple febrile seizure
Reassurance and safety-netting -- most children outgrow the tendency and it does not cause brain damage
Rescue benzodiazepine plan if seizures are recurrent or prolonged

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
